Agreed on synthetic stress plan across regions and an action list to finalize pilot config.
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-04-06
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: 58 minutes
Location: Zoom
Record: yes

Attendees:
- Laura Chen, Redwood (AE)
- Miguel Alvarez, Redwood (SE)
- Anita Rao, Redwood (CSM) (brief intro)
- Samir Patel, Delta Bank (SRE)
- Ruth Kim, Delta Bank (Lead ML Eng)
- Priya Desai, Delta Bank (PM)
- Omar Hussein, Delta Bank (Platform)

[00:00] Laura: Okay, everyone, thanks for joining, we want to run through the throughput checkpoints and then get into autoscale playbook decisions. Quick check: everyone's on mute?

[00:18] Samir: Yep, Samir here. We got the bench artifacts you sent — thanks. Had a quick skim prior to this.

[00:30] Miguel: Great. I'll start with the bench recap, then we can dig into policies. Reminder: these runs used the H100-heavy pool we spun up in Dedicated, quantized to 4-bit with the fast-kernel path.

[01:00] Miguel: Topline — steady-state throughput at 65 tokens/sec per GPU for the 2k-seq doc parser, p99 latency around 420ms in the region we tested. But during the 2-minute spike test we saw queuing and p99 jump to ~1.4s when we hit sustained 3x baseline.

[01:40] Ruth: Wait, you said 65 tokens/sec — is that wall time or token generation? Our production token length is longer, average 1.7k tokens per request, so we need to map that.

[02:05] Miguel: Good call. That's generation tokens; effective throughput for you with 1.7k averager is approx 0.038 requests/sec per GPU. Which means to meet your target of 200 reqs/minute we'd need ~88 GPUs in steady state, ignoring KV cache and batching gains.

[02:40] Priya: Can you walk through how batching and KV cache change that number? In our product we have many repeated prefixes for KYC forms.

[03:00] Miguel: Absolutely. With prefix caching (we mimicked your prefix distribution — thanks, Ruth), effective token decode reduces by about 20-30% for common forms. Batching also helps — with 40ms batching window and continuous batching we simulated a 1.6x throughput uplift. So the 88 GPUs could drop to the mid-50s in idealized conditions. But that depends on latency SLO tolerance.

[03:40] Samir: That's big. But we operate under a 600ms p95 SLO. If batching adds latency jitter that might push us past the SLO for interactive parts of the flow.

[04:10] Laura: Right. That's the classic latency vs cost play. We typically recommended a mixed approach: keep min pool sized for base steady traffic to hit p95 and let autoscale handle bursts, but also include a small pre-warm policy for known traffic windows.

[04:35] Miguel: To expand — policy options we discussed: queue-length based autoscale, CPU/GPU utilization threshold, request-rate per GPU, and time-of-day scheduled pre-warm. All have pros/cons. For Delta Bank I'd suggest queue-length + scheduled pre-warm for morning batch windows.

[05:05] Omar: What's the overhead of pre-warm? If we schedule +20 GPUs 15 minutes prior, do we pay full-hour increments or is it on-second billing?

[05:25] Laura: For Dedicated pilot billing, we show pro-rata billing per minute in the pilot terms — not full-hour for the pilot. In production committed pools are monthly, but for pilot we can do pro-rated. We will include precise numbers in the pricing sheet.

[05:55] Ruth: I want to talk model variants — do we have a cheaper quantized variant we can route to for lower-latency cases? Like a 3B distilled model or a quantized 8-bit?

[06:18] Miguel: Yes. We validated a 7B quantized route that used ~40% less GPU time and reduced p99 by ~200ms on the short docs. But accuracy on some corner cases dropped ~1.8% on entity extraction. For KYC that's borderline. We can do A/B but you'd need fallback policies.

[06:50] Priya: So fallback means if the distilled route returns low confidence we send to the larger model? That adds cost and latency.

[07:00] Miguel: Exactly. Redwood supports function-level routing and fallback. We can set confidence thresholds and spawn a second call async or sync depending on your latency tolerance. But it does complicate cost math.

[07:30] Samir: Back to scaling: in the 2-minute spike where p99 went to 1.4s, did the system attempt to spin new GPUs or was it queue growth because the autoscaler cooldown is long?

[07:50] Miguel: That was the latter — autoscaler cooldown of 120s plus warmup times for new GPU instances meant the rps sustained queued and caused the p99 spike. We tested shorter cooldowns but saw oscillation when traffic is spiky. That's where burst override and short-lived pre-warm pool are helpful.

[08:25] Laura: We can configure a burst tier — a reserved small buffer of warm GPUs that sit idle but ready, plus an ephemeral burst that can be over-provisioned for 5-15 minutes. For pilot, recommended approach: min=24 GPUs, reserve burst pool=10 GPUs for immediate headroom, max=120, with autoscale based on 95th-percentile queue-length threshold.

[09:05] Ruth: Min 24 feels high vs the earlier 55/88 numbers. What's the reasoning?

[09:15] Miguel: The 88 was naive steady-state if no prefix cache/batching. With your prefix patterns + batching it's realistic to target mid-40s, but min should cover your low baseline plus redundancy and regional split. Also the 24 is for one region — you plan two regions (NA and EU) for resiliency, so combined baseline is higher.

[09:45] Priya: On regional split — if we route 60/40 NA/EU, can autoscale be global or per-region?

[09:58] Miguel: Redwood Dedicated autoscale is per-pool; you can create regional pools and a smart routing layer that directs traffic by affinity. Autoscale acts per pool. We recommend per-region pools to limit cross-region latency and comply with data residency.

[10:30] Omar: Security question — for pre-warm GPUs we need to ensure no customer data is loaded into cache. Does pre-warm initialize KV cache with any corp data?

[10:50] Miguel: Pre-warm does not populate customer KV by default. It simply keeps the model processes and kernels resident. We do not seed caches with PII. If you want to pre-populate, that's an opt-in step and would require keying off tokens you provide and replicating in staging under your VPC.

[11:15] Samir: Good. For compliance we'll keep pre-warm clean. If we need warm caches for known prefixes we can do safe synthetic prefixes that do not include customer data.

[11:30] Laura: On fallback and routing: one pattern is to route low-confidence results to async reprocessing so user-facing flows aren't blocked. That might suit your KYC flows where you can show a provisional status then reconcile.

[11:55] Priya: That sounds feasible for secondary verification flows. For primary acceptance we need p95 under 600ms. So how many GPUs and which policy will guarantee that?

[12:15] Miguel: With batching constrained to 30ms window and prefix caching, we simulated p95 ~ 420ms at 60% utilization. So keep steady-state utilization target at 60-70% to maintain p95. That translates into the min pool numbers I mentioned. If you accept slightly higher cost we can lower that utilization target.

[12:45] Ruth: What's your recommendation for cooldown / scale step sizes to avoid oscillation?

[12:55] Miguel: Recommend scale step increase of 10-15 GPUs, cooldown 90s for scale up, 300s for scale down, and a queue-length threshold at 75 requests to trigger a scale-up. Those numbers are adjustable based on bench results.

[13:20] Samir: If we do scale-down 300s, do we risk leaving too many warm GPUs idle and paying for them?

[13:30] Laura: For pilot we'll monitor cost and can tune down the reserved burst or lower the min if cost is unacceptable. Also, pilot billing is pro-rated so you'll see actual cost impact in the next bill.

[14:00] Miguel: One more note — we saw kernel contention with mixed model types on the same GPU node in the bench. For the pilot it's safer to homogenous pools per model variant to avoid slowdowns.

[14:20] Priya: So separate pools for big model and distilled model, with routing rules?

[14:25] Miguel: Correct. That simplifies scheduling and gives predictable latency.

[14:40] Ruth: How do we measure quality regressions if we A/B to distilled? We need an eval harness integrated into the pipeline.

[14:50] Miguel: We can instrument an eval set and run lightweight evals on sample outputs, plus Redwood Optimize can alert on regression thresholds. We'll include a sample eval config in the follow-up docs.

[15:10] Samir: Regarding the synthetic bench run you proposed — can you run a multi-region test that warms caches and simulates our morning spike pattern? We want to see tail latencies when two regions spike simultaneously.

[15:30] Miguel: Yes, we'll do that. We'll add prefix-cache warm-up sequences to simulate your repeated forms. We'll include both H100 and A100 mixes. Expect artifacts by 2027-04-10.

[15:45] Laura: On pricing, I'll send an updated Dedicated pool breakdown: min pool cost, burst reserve cost, ephemeral burst cost per hour, and an estimated monthly band. That will be in the sheet Monday.

[16:05] Priya: Also can you include a sensitivity table showing 10/20/30% batching and cache uplift on cost and latency?

[16:15] Laura: Yup, we'll add a sensitivity section.

[16:30] Omar: A question — if we enable autoscale based on queue-length, how do we surface traceability to our on-call? We need logs and metrics pushed to our prometheus/grafana stack or to Datadog.

[16:45] Miguel: Redwood Console can push metrics to Datadog and you can also pull Prometheus exporters. We'll surface token-level cost, GPU utilization, queue length, and per-model p95/p99. We'll include the Grafana dashboards in the deliverables.

[17:10] Ruth: On the security front, we need SAML SSO for the console and KMS integration, plus audit logs retained 90 days for pilot. Is that supported?

[17:25] Laura: SAML and KMS are supported for private deployments; for Dedicated pilot we can enable SSO with limited roles and provide audit log exports for 90 days. I'll attach the security matrix in the follow-up.

[17:40] Samir: Ok good. One more thing: for failover, if a region is overwhelmed can Redwood route to the other region's dedicated pool?

[17:55] Miguel: Yes, via smart routing. You can set policies for latency thresholds and fallback to the other region or to a cheaper hosted model. But cross-region routing may hit data residency concerns — you'll want to keep PII flows in-region.

[18:20] Priya: Let's document the allowed fallback paths before enabling auto-failover.

[18:35] Laura: Agreed, we'll draft a failover playbook and include recommended guardrails.

[18:45] Anita: Quick admin note — I'll create the shared drive folder and invite everyone; Miguel will drop bench artifacts and the pre-warm script there.

[19:00] Miguel: I'll also include a small script that runs a staged prefix-warm and bench harness you can run from your CI.

[19:15] Samir: For the synthetic bench, please include raw logs with timestamps and a CSV summary of p95/p99 numbers per minute.

[19:30] Miguel: Will do.

[19:45] Laura: To recap, deliverables: pricing sheet, burst policy spreadsheet, synthetic multi-region bench artifacts, eval config, security matrix, and a follow-up call next Monday to finalize autoscale numbers.

[20:05] Priya: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.

[20:15] Ruth: Thanks.

[20:20] Samir: Thanks.

[20:25] Laura: End of meeting.

Notes on transcript quality: some proper nouns were inferred (kernel names, product nicknames), occasional mis-hearings ("KV catch" for KV cache, "Red wood" for Redwood). Crosstalk minimal. The transcript retains pauses and filler language to preserve realism.
